subject: Architecture
title: Buildings and Climate Change
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Buildings and Climate Change.

hook.text: Buildings produce nearly 40% of global carbon emissions — more than all cars, trucks, and planes combined.

buildup.text: Heating, cooling, and lighting buildings burns fossil fuels around the clock, year after year.

discovery.text: Operational energy is only half the story. Making cement alone produces 8% of global CO₂ emissions.

twist.text: Most buildings standing in 2050 are already built today. Retrofitting them matters more than new construction.

climax.text: Architecture has a bigger climate impact than aviation — yet gets far less public scrutiny.

punchline.text: We debate flights and cars. The real offender is your building.

quiz.question: What percentage of global carbon emissions do buildings produce?

details.summary: Buildings account for roughly 40% of global energy consumption and 33% of greenhouse gas emissions. From manufacturing materials like cement and steel to heating, cooling, and lighting occupied spaces, the built environment is climate change's largest and most overlooked contributor.
details.whyItMatters: You can't address climate change without addressing buildings. Architecture is both a major part of the problem and a massive opportunity for solutions.
takeaways: Buildings produce roughly 40% of global energy consumption
Construction materials and operations drive 33% of emissions
Every new building locks in energy patterns for decades

faq.question: Which part of a building's lifecycle produces the most emissions?
faq.answer: Operations (heating, cooling, lighting) typically account for 60-80% of lifetime emissions for conventional buildings. However, as buildings become more energy-efficient, the embodied carbon in construction materials becomes proportionally more significant, sometimes exceeding operational carbon.

faq.question: Can renovating old buildings help more than building new ones?
faq.answer: Often yes. Retrofitting existing buildings avoids the huge embodied carbon cost of demolition and new construction. The greenest building is frequently the one already standing. Deep energy retrofits can reduce operational emissions by 50-75% at a fraction of new construction's carbon cost.
